idiom_name: implicit / given type-class resolution (Ordering, Numeric) summoned from the static type
implementation_notes: Scala's implicit (Scala 2) and given (Scala 3) resolution is a compile-time search keyed by the static type of the requested instance, so behaviour is selected from types in exactly the way tag dispatching selects from a tag type - the compiler picks the instance and passes it as an ordinary argument (a dictionary) unless inlining erases it. The standard library's Ordering[T] and Numeric[T] are the canonical tag classes: one abstract type plus per-type instances, summoned through a context bound ([T: Ordering]) or explicitly with summon/implicitly, with the type class documentation noting that instances can be defined anywhere, including for types you do not own. What replaces the classic structure: context bounds plus given/implicit instances replace the overload ladder, and 'more specific instance wins' replaces inheritance ranking (instance selection follows the implicit scope, not a specificity ladder, so ambiguity is resolved by scope rules rather than by tag inheritance). The classic form is still justified when selection must be based on constraint subsumption or when a library must avoid implicit scope entirely (Scala 3 even requires explicit imports for givens outside the companion objects to curb leakage).
pitfalls: Implicit search consults the implicit scope (companions of the types involved), so an instance can be picked without being imported and can silently win over the expected one; ambiguity is a compile error only when both candidates are equally eligible.

Implicit conversions (the old view bounds) turn unexpected members into calls and are widely treated as dangerous - use a type class with an explicit operation, not a conversion, when adding behaviour to a type you do not own.

Handing the dictionary around is not free by construction: unless the compiler inlines and erases the instance argument, the 'zero-overhead' property depends on the optimizer, and the devirtualized path can still be a megamorphic call for many instances.

Type inference and given/implicit overloading interact: an inferred instance type that is too general (e.g. Numeric[Any]) selects an unintended implementation, a class of bug that reads as 'the wrong arithmetic ran'.
